rationale:
This edition restates the judgment; it does not change it. The incumbent was over the reader's budget in the article, in the first sentences of three header answers and in the best conventional explanation, so this candidate retells the article within the ceiling and returns a complete assessment. No verdict changed. Every per-claim verdict, the case verdict (unresolved), the load-bearing and weakest-link sets, the component states and the research priority are carried over unchanged, because no record admitted since the incumbent moves any of them.

What changed in the assessment. Each header answer now opens with the answer itself: what is claimed; that the dispute is light versus emulsion flaw; and the coma and flash-calibration tests. The scene-setting clauses are gone. The best conventional explanation, synthesis and steelman are compressed to the same content. Component labels and notes are rewritten in plain words and carry no record ids, since a reader meets them before the article. Record ids now appear only in the synthesis, steelman, reasoning and objection fields. There each is named beside the claim it is attached to, or disclosed as a parent or sibling basis. Two reasonings in the prior pattern cited records against claims they are not attached to: the alignments claim and the flash-sharpness claim. Those now describe the related material without spending its id.

What changed in the article. It follows the same structure, in this order: the events; the four accounts; common ground; the defect case; the original glass; the case for light; the statistics; which near-Earth account; and what would change our mind. It is told more tightly, and repetition across the statistics sections is cut. The Castle Yankee sentence no longer says the high-confidence nuclear sample is dominated by one night. The evidence for that proportion was declined at intake, so the article now reports only the unchecked claim and the audit that could test it. Held-on-source-only claims are told as reports throughout: the defect rate, flash sharpness, the geomagnetic trend, the alignments, the altitude range and the Castle Yankee projection. Ledger vocabulary is removed. All three incumbent plates are kept.

What stayed the same. The featured set is unchanged: the thesis and its attribution steps, the crux, each competing account's deciding claims (the defect rate, the copy genealogy, natural-body exclusion, the toy-model argument), and the population statistics with their own controls. The map of the controversy has not moved. The crux order is unchanged, with the coma validation leading as the only physical light-versus-flaw test. No research item was settled. The article tells the same four accounts as the accounts field, one per paragraph. The packet carries no reader notes, objections or panel dissent.
article:
The first great photographic atlas of the sky carries marks nobody has yet explained. On glass plates exposed at Palomar Observatory in the early 1950s, years before any satellite flew, astronomers have catalogued star-like points that appear on one exposure and never again. The boldest reading is that some were sunlight glinting off artificial objects in orbit before Sputnik. The evidence so far establishes less, but not nothing. The marks are physically real, and the most famous ones are reported on the original telescope negative rather than a later copy. Statistical patterns in the population hold up in the proponents' own catalog but not in one rebuilt from scratch. What remains open is the question under all the others: whether any of these marks was made by light at all, rather than by a flaw in the photographic emulsion.

## Nine lights, one night

On 12 April 1950 the 48-inch Schmidt telescope on Palomar Mountain exposed a red-sensitive plate for about fifty minutes. Seventy years later the VASCO project (Vanishing and Appearing Sources during a Century of Observations), led by astronomer Beatriz Villarroel, reported on it [nine star-like points within about ten arcminutes, absent from the overlapping plate taken six days later and from far deeper modern surveys]{claim=TRN-C001}. The discovery paper named an unknown plate contamination as its first candidate explanation. It offered brief sunlight reflections from objects near geosynchronous orbit as another, if contamination could be excluded.

{plate:IMG-TRN-P01}

A second event followed: [three points of about 16th magnitude, within ten arcseconds of one another, on a plate from 19 July 1952, gone from the next exposure within the hour and absent from all later imaging down to magnitude 25.5]{claim=TRN-C003}. The project has since built a working catalog of about 107,875 single-exposure candidates, and most of the argument now happens there.

## Four accounts of a dot

Every explanation must account for the same thing: a small, round, dark grain on glass.

**Plate defects.** Emulsion does not need the sky to make a dot. Critics note that decades of searching old plates for flashes from gamma-ray bursts ended without one confident find. They argue that [ordinary emulsion, copying and scanning flaws make star-like marks often enough to contaminate any search for one-time flashes]{claim=TRN-C101}, a rate asserted but never measured. The account predicts candidates that resemble known defects and gather in plate corners and edges, and population patterns that fade when the catalog is rebuilt.

**Artificial glints.** The proponents hold that [some marks are sunlight reflected from objects near Earth, at roughly geosynchronous height]{claim=TRN-C021], and that [artificial objects able to make them were in orbit before Sputnik 1]{claim=TRN-C022}. The strong form adds that [they were extraterrestrial technology]{claim=TRN-C023}. It predicts sharp images, fewer candidates inside Earth's shadow, groupings, and signals that strengthen as defects are filtered out.

**Natural bodies near Earth.** One preprint accepts real near-Earth flashes but proposes icy dust clumping into metre-scale aggregates after geomagnetic storms. It shares the shadow prediction and differs on size and makeup.

**Exotic physics.** A dark-matter proposal takes the flashes' reality as its premise and says nothing about defects. It inherits the central question rather than answering it.

Most of the evidence cannot separate the second account from the third. Beneath all of them lies one question: [whether any mark was made by light entering the telescope during the exposure]{claim=TRN-C020}, rather than added later in the emulsion, the copying or the scan.

## What nobody disputes

Start with what the critics concede. Hambly is an astronomer at the Royal Observatory Edinburgh and an author of one of the survey's two major digitizations. He put Edinburgh's glass copy under a microscope, and the nine marks are there at the reported positions; they are not scanner glitches. [An outside researcher's pipeline, written without the discoverers' software or lists, recovers eight of the nine, all three from 1952, and about two-thirds of the 5,399-candidate public catalog]{claim=TRN-C004}. The marks are real. The question is what makes a mark.

{plate:IMG-TRN-P02}

## The case for defects

Hambly and his coauthor Blair give the conventional account its strongest form. Their inspection found emulsion holes, bubbles and scratch-like marks on the copy plates, and appear-once detections on the neighbouring field too.

They measured that [the nine 1950 marks are sharper and more concentrated than stars of the same brightness, all nine on the sharp side of the plate's distribution]{claim=TRN-C002}. The odds of that, if they were stars, are of order one in a billion. A classifier files them with spurious detections. But its spurious class is defined by having no modern counterpart, which is also what defines a transient, so a real flash would be labelled artifact-like by construction.

Then comes the family tree of the copies. Two modern digitizations both show the candidates, and that agreement seemed to rule out simple flaws. But both [descend from copy negatives printed from the same intermediate positive, so one flaw made at that step would appear in both]{claim=TRN-C007}. “Two independent datasets” turns out to mean two cousins.

{plate:IMG-TRN-P03}

The account carries two debts. Nobody has measured how often copying mints star-like fakes, and it cannot reach plates outside the Palomar family.

## The original glass

Only the original negative sits above the shared copy. A preprint by J. Yang and Beatriz Villarroel, not yet peer reviewed, reports microscopy of the negative that was in the telescope on 12 April 1950, now at the Caltech archive, registered star by star against the digitization. It also examines a Harvard copy of the 1952 plate. It finds [all nine 1950 sources on the original negative at their published positions]{claim=TRN-C024}, and the 1952 triple on the copy and in the original digitization. For the flagship events, the cousins are answered by the grandparent. The copying argument keeps its force only for the hundred thousand uninspected candidates.

There the good news stops, for everyone. The study states that microscopy cannot tell a brief flash from a flaw born in the emulsion, because single dots of both kinds look alike. Hambly himself directed the microscopist who examined the plate to the nine. The microscopist found them un-star-like and judged emulsion defects a reasonable attribution, noting that the field lies in a plate corner, where defects are commoner. The study prints that opinion against its own interest. It argues that, judged against steady stars, a sub-second flash *should* look like a defect. The clean escape would be the same flash caught at a second observatory at the same instant, and it is closed: no such plate exists.

The examination was not blind and has not been repeated outside the group. “Original or copy?” has an answer for these events; “sky or chemistry?” does not.

## The case for light

The proponents answer the sharpness finding with physics. A star sits on the plate for the whole exposure, smeared by air and tracking. They argue that [a flash under a second long has no time to smear and should look sharper and rounder than a star]{claim=TRN-C102}. It is a derivation, not a measurement: nobody has exposed period emulsion to controlled flashes and drawn the curve. Until someone does, sharpness is the case's most-cited observation and its least decisive.

The stronger development comes from outside Palomar. Ivo Busko, a retired Space Telescope Science Institute developer, searched same-night plate pairs from Hamburg Observatory. He reports [appear-once candidates with narrow profiles on a different telescope, emulsion, archive and digitization]{claim=TRN-C010}. The copying argument cannot touch them. Without a candidate rate against matched controls, though, “the same phenomenon” and “the same weakness of old emulsions” look alike.

His follow-up uses a Hamburg telescope with strong coma, the small comet-shaped smear its optics give to off-axis light. He reports that [candidate images carry the coma pattern expected of light through the optics]{claim=TRN-C011}. Scratches and chemistry do not know where the optical axis is; light does. If validated blind against known defects and deliberately made flashes, this would be a detector of real light usable on any archive. It has not been validated, it covers Hamburg only, and the paper says its data do not establish where the light came from.

## The statistics

Above the single events sits an argument from the whole catalog. The record here is mixed in a useful way: who reproduces what is its most informative feature.

### The shadow

[The catalog shows fewer candidates inside Earth's shadow at geosynchronous height than geometry expects — about 0.46% against 1.4%]{claim=TRN-C005}. A sunlit reflector goes dark in the shadow; a defect does not. It is the best geometric evidence either near-Earth account has, and they share it.

A statistician working from the proponents' supplied rows with his own code reproduces it; he later joined the group. A machine-learning study scoring candidates for defect-likeness finds [the shortfall stronger at every assumed altitude once defect-like rows are removed]{claim=TRN-C129}. A modelling preprint fits the shortfall's shape to shells at different heights and gets a poor fit. It states [a characteristic height of about 20,000–35,000 km]{claim=TRN-C108}, which its authors call a spread across choices, not a confidence interval.

Against this, Watters and colleagues, several of whom work in UAP-research organizations, show that the uniform background the test assumes is false. Candidates rise toward plate corners and edges and gather in clusters and voids. Under a proper null, in closely related datasets, the shortfall is not significant. At least 91% of the rows used belong to a set once removed for lying within 5 arcseconds of catalogued stars. The proponents reply that the critics' subset is twenty times smaller and underpowered. Their modelling preprint concedes part of the point, cutting its sky region to avoid empty stripes and edge effects that “may influence the results.” And the filter that strengthens the signal is the group's own classifier, trained on its own visual judgments. Removing defect-like rows sharpens any signal that defects dilute, whether or not what remains is sky.

### The bombs

[Candidate rates are higher within a day of atmospheric nuclear tests — a relative risk of about 1.45]{claim=TRN-C006}. On the supplied rows it survives weather and moonlight controls, a permutation test and the machine-learning filter. An open Bayesian reanalysis that allows for day-to-day correlation also finds it, though weaker. Another preprint reports that [candidate rates fall with geomagnetic activity, and that allowing for this strengthens the nuclear link]{claim=TRN-C103}; its figures have not been checked here. A companion test finds that star counts and limiting magnitude do not change with storms, closing one route to a spurious pattern.

But the one catalog rebuilt from whole-plate scans, by Hayes, finds no significant effect once nightly sky coverage is modelled. The relative risk is 1.35 with an interval that includes no effect, and 1.03 in the exposure-weighted model. Watters traces the timing mostly to the observing schedule. The hotspot preprint also reports, in a passage not yet checked here, that [all 203 high-probability candidates from the night before the Castle Yankee test project onto Pacific regions]{claim=TRN-C125}. Those are one night's plates, which a direct audit could examine.

The pattern is the tell: the correlations reproduce on the proponents' catalog and fade when the catalog is rebuilt. That does not prove them artifacts; it makes the catalog the battleground. And even a surviving nuclear link would fit fallout reaching the plates as well as glinting objects.

### The hotspots

The newest result projects high-probability candidates along the line of sight onto a shell at 35,786 km and asks which patch of Earth each hangs over. [Sixteen of 137 patches hold more candidates than the group's random control, after correcting for testing many patches at once]{claim=TRN-C119}. Most lie over the eastern Pacific west of southern Mexico and over the southern Gulf of Mexico. [Fourteen draw their excess from at least two plates]{claim=TRN-C132}; [two adjacent patches draw theirs from a single plate]{claim=TRN-C133}.

Three things limit it. Every location depends on the assumed height; at the 20,000 km the companion fit prefers, the candidates fall elsewhere. The excess is measured inside the same catalog and filter, so a plate rich in defects sends its excess wherever the geometry points. And the clustering method fails its own control: [random positions put through the same procedure meet the authors' threshold for non-random clustering]{claim=TRN-C122}, in only three control runs. Separately, [some groups of candidates are reported to fall in straight lines]{claim=TRN-C104}, from a paper this site has not read in full. A second preprint finds lines beyond chance on seven plates, using a criterion chosen after the fact.

## Which near-Earth?

Suppose the near-Earth geometry held. The modelling preprint argues that [dusty-plasma grains a millimetre across cannot make the centimetre-to-metre reflecting surfaces its brightness model infers]{claim=TRN-C117}. That size estimate rests on assumed height, mirror-like reflection, flash duration and reflectivity. It also rests on a catalog that excluded bright sources, which, the authors concede, biases sizes downward. The same preprint finds [no robust link between candidate dates and annual meteor showers]{claim=TRN-C116}, closing one natural route.

It then argues that [among the models it tried — natural bodies, dusty plasma, non-human intelligence — only the last fits all five reported features]{claim=TRN-C118]. The five are sharp profiles, groupings, the shadow shortfall, nuclear timing, and the geomagnetic pattern. That is fit among a hand-picked set, built on features contested at the catalog level, and the authors add that nature can always surprise us. The hotspot paper's authors call the intelligence reading “unfortunately not falsifiable.” Nothing in the record tests an extraterrestrial origin. Even a proven pre-Sputnik object would need a separate argument before that word earned its place.

## Where the support thins

The marks are on the plates, and independent software finds them: settled. The flagship nine are on the original negative: reported, awaiting review. The population patterns describe the sky: contested, surviving only in the catalog where they were found. Some mark was made by light: unresolved, and everything above depends on it. The light came from near Earth: unresolved. Artificial objects orbited before Sputnik: the headline, unresolved. They were extraterrestrial: not testable now, by its proponents' own account.

## What would change our mind

Toward light:
- a blind test of the coma signature that separates deliberately made flashes from the full range of defects;
- a calibration on period emulsion showing the nine marks match sub-second flashes and not flaws;
- a shadow shortfall in an independently extracted catalog, under a preregistered null that models the plate background as it is.

Toward defects:
- a measured count of star-like flaws per copying stage, at the rates the catalog needs;
- the Castle Yankee-night candidates concentrated on one or two plates, with edge clustering and defect shapes;
- the coma test failing;
- Hamburg-style candidate rates that match defect rates on matched controls.

Between the two near-Earth accounts: an altitude that survives independent shadow code and orbital motion, and a size estimate that does not depend on excluding the brightest candidates.

Microscopy of single dots has done what it can. Three things still discriminate: the coma signature, statistics on catalogs nobody's thumb has touched, and, for any future flash, simultaneous imaging from two or more stations. That last turns one ambiguous dot into a measured distance or a local artifact.

assessment.synthesis: The case verdict is unresolved: the marks are real plate features, but nothing yet decides whether any was made by light through the telescope rather than by an emulsion flaw. The observation level is secure. The 1950 nine are confirmed by the critics on the Edinburgh copy (TRN-E002, on TRN-C001) and recovered by an independent pipeline (TRN-E008, on TRN-C004). They are reported on the original Caltech negative (TRN-E022, on TRN-C024), which removes the copy-chain route of TRN-C007 (TRN-E005) for the two flagship events (TRN-E023). The crux TRN-C020 has narrowed from original-or-copy to flash-or-flaw. The microscopy authors concede their method cannot decide it, and their microscopist leaned defect (TRN-E024). Sharpness (TRN-C002, TRN-E003) is a sound measurement read two ways (TRN-E004, TRN-E006) without calibration. The two mechanisms that would decide the crux, flash sharpness (TRN-C102) and defect rates (TRN-C101), are both held on their anchors alone. The coma signature (TRN-E014, on TRN-C011) is the one physical discriminant, and it is unvalidated. The population claims split by replication type. They survive reanalysis of the author-supplied rows (TRN-E010 and TRN-E015 on TRN-C005 and TRN-C006; TRN-E052 on TRN-C129). They fail an independent extraction and a corrected null (TRN-E009 on TRN-C006; TRN-E011 on both). The modelling preprint concedes part of the background objection (TRN-E051, on TRN-C005), and the hotspot paper's random controls meet its clustering criterion (TRN-E079, on TRN-C122). That pattern indicts the catalog, not yet the sky. Attribution inherits all of it. TRN-E074 assumes near-Earth origin, and TRN-E020 offers a natural route sharing the geometry (both on TRN-C021). TRN-E038's exclusion of that route (TRN-C117) rests on a size inference its authors call biased by bright-source exclusion (TRN-C111; TRN-E062, TRN-E063). The proponents call the intelligence reading unfalsifiable (TRN-E083). The single record whose removal would most change the case is TRN-E011, the only strong record against the shadow deficit. Without it TRN-C005 would rise to provisionally supported and TRN-C021 with it, leaving TRN-C020 untouched; the case verdict would survive.
assessment.steelman: Nine sharp, round marks lie within ten arcminutes of one another on one fifty-minute exposure. They are reported on the original telescope negative (TRN-E022) and are absent from the overlapping plate six days later (TRN-E002). A second event puts three sixteenth-magnitude points within ten arcseconds that vanish within the hour and never return to magnitude 25.5 (TRN-E007). The proponents read the nine marks' sharpness as what a sub-second flash should leave on a long exposure (TRN-E006). The defect account has no measured rate for clustered, star-like flaws on original negatives (TRN-C101 is held on its anchor). The defect account must also explain several things together. The shadow and nuclear-window signals persist and grow under a classifier trained to remove defects (TRN-E015; TRN-E052 and TRN-E053 on TRN-C129). One environmental route to a spurious timing pattern tests negative (TRN-E017, on TRN-C006). An archive with no shared ancestry shows narrow-profiled candidates (TRN-E013) that carry, on the author's reading, the coma signature of light through the optics (TRN-E014). No single defect mechanism in the record accounts for clustering, sharpness, filter-strengthening and cross-archive recurrence together. This assessment does not answer that conjunction. It holds that each element is separately undercut — unblinded, uncalibrated, same-catalog, unvalidated — and that a conjunction of undercut elements is not yet evidence.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: Some one-time, star-like marks on 1950s Palomar survey plates were real flashes of light through the telescope, and in the strong version, sunlight glints off artificial objects orbiting before Sputnik. Proponents go further and propose an extraterrestrial origin, which they themselves call unfalsifiable.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: The dispute is whether any mark was made by light entering the telescope rather than by a flaw in the emulsion — something microscopy cannot decide and no calibration yet measures. Both sides accept the marks exist; the flagship nine are confirmed on copy glass and reported on the original negative. The population patterns — fewer candidates in Earth's shadow, timing near nuclear tests, clusters over Earth — hold on the proponents' own catalog, and the two tested independently did not survive. If the near-Earth geometry held, nothing yet separates artificial reflectors from natural ones.
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: Blind-test the coma signature — the distortion telescope optics stamp on real light — against known defects and deliberate flashes, and calibrate how flashes look on period emulsion. Those would decide light versus flaw. Then reproduce the Earth-shadow shortfall on an independently built catalog, under a preregistered null that models the plate background as it is. Artificial origin would need a size or structure argument not built on a catalog that excluded bright sources. Extraterrestrial origin has no test on the table.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: Photographic archives make star-like marks without any sky event: emulsion flaws, development chemistry and handling damage. For this survey, defects on the shared intermediate positive from which both major digitizations descend mean one copying flaw appears “independently” twice. The critics found emulsion holes, bubbles and scratch-like marks on the copy plates, and appear-once detections on the neighbouring field. The microscopist who examined the original 1950 negative judged emulsion defects a reasonable attribution, in a plate corner where defects gather. On this account, the population patterns belong to an unvalidated working catalog, at least 91% of whose rows were earlier set aside as lying near catalogued stars. The observing schedule and a plate background that rises toward corners and edges do the rest. The patterns reproduce when the rows are reused and vanish when the catalog is rebuilt. The account's unpaid debts: no measured rate for star-like defects, and no reach over an independent archive whose candidates reportedly carry the optical signature of real light.

components.label: The marks are real features of the plates
components.note: The critics confirmed them on copy glass and an independent pipeline recovered them. Both camps accept this.

components.label: The flagship events sit on the original negative
components.note: One unreviewed, unblinded microscopy study reports it. It removes the copying explanation for these two events only.

components.label: Some mark was made by light through the telescope
components.note: The crux. Microscopy cannot tell flash from flaw, the coma test is unvalidated, and flash sharpness and defect rates are both unmeasured.

components.label: Population patterns: shadow, nuclear timing, hotspots
components.note: They hold on the proponents' catalog but fail on an independently rebuilt one and under a corrected background model. The group's own controls undercut the clustering.

components.label: A reflecting population near Earth, and its height
components.note: It rests on the disputed shadow shortfall. The height range is not a confidence interval, and natural and artificial versions share the geometry.

components.label: Artificial and extraterrestrial origin
components.note: Pre-Sputnik hardware depends on the unresolved steps below it. Its proponents call the intelligence reading unfalsifiable.

researchPriority.reason: Several cheap, unrun tests on existing scans could decide the population statistics, and two lab tests reach the light-versus-flaw question that no existing measurement settles.

claimAssessments.reasoning: Depends on TRN-C020 and TRN-C021, both unresolved. The two attached records are weak and qualifying. TRN-E018 reports alignments on seven plates whose marks inherit the catalog's provenance problem. TRN-E020 proposes a natural near-Earth population that would satisfy the same geometry without hardware. Nothing in the record bears on artificiality directly; the verdict rests on the dependency structure, not on a test.

treatment.plainLanguage: Artificial objects able to make these marks were near Earth before Sputnik 1 was launched in October 1957.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If established it would decide against both the defect and the natural-body accounts at once; it cannot be reached without first settling TRN-C020 and TRN-C021.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E020's natural icy-aggregate mechanism fits the same shadow geometry, so even a vindicated near-Earth population would not select artificial objects.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A near-Earth population established on an independent catalog, plus a size or structure constraint natural aggregates cannot meet that does not depend on excluding bright sources
Contemporaneous plates from a second observatory recording the same flash with a parallax consistent with orbital distance

claimAssessments.reasoning: No test in the record can bear on it. The hotspot preprint's authors call the intelligence interpretation 'unfortunately not falsifiable' (TRN-E083). They offer replication at other observatories only as a way to clarify interpretation (TRN-E084). The claim also depends on TRN-C022, itself unresolved. The toy-model argument of TRN-C118 is graded separately and is not a test.

treatment.plainLanguage: The reflecting objects were technology made by a non-human intelligence from beyond Earth.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Nothing observable in the record distinguishes it from other artificial or natural reflectors; its own proponents concede it cannot be falsified (TRN-E083).
treatment.strongestObjection: Even a proven pre-Sputnik object would need a separate origin argument, and TRN-C022 is not established.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A stated, preregistered observation whose outcome the extraterrestrial reading forbids and the alternatives allow
A resolved image or spectrum of a pre-1957 reflector inconsistent with any natural body

claimAssessments.reasoning: The only attached support, TRN-E074, is the modelling preprint's estimate that a third of the sample is solar reflection. That estimate is inferred from the shadow deficit the paper assumes real. TRN-E020 qualifies by offering a natural near-Earth route. TRN-E021 is context that presumes the flashes real. The claim therefore rests on TRN-C005, which is mixed, and on TRN-C020, which is unresolved.

treatment.plainLanguage: At least some flashes were sunlight bouncing off objects close to Earth, at roughly the height of geosynchronous orbit, not light from distant stars.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Against the defect account it would be highly diagnostic; against the natural-body account it discriminates nothing, since both predict the same shadow geometry.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E011, on the shadow deficit TRN-C005 on which this claim rests, finds no significant deficit once the plate background is modelled as non-uniform.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A shadow shortfall in an independently extracted catalog under a preregistered background model
A preregistered altitude fit with orbital dynamics returning a formal confidence interval on independent data

claimAssessments.reasoning: The crux. TRN-E024 establishes that microscopy of single sources cannot separate a flash from an emulsion defect, and its microscopist leaned defect. TRN-E014 reports a coma signature on Hamburg candidates, a potential incident-light test, but it is unvalidated. TRN-E004 and TRN-E011 undermine. TRN-E006 argues that sharpness is expected of flashes but measures nothing. Neither deciding mechanism, TRN-C101 or TRN-C102, has been measured, so no record decides the claim in either direction.

treatment.plainLanguage: At least some marks were made by light coming through the telescope during the exposure, not by flaws introduced in the emulsion, the copying or the scanning.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every attribution claim above it is conditional on this; it is what separates the defect account from all three real-flash accounts.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E024: the one specialist to examine the original 1950 negative for this purpose judged emulsion defects a reasonable attribution.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blind validation of the coma discriminant against known defects and deliberately produced flashes
A flash-profile calibration on period emulsion that matches or excludes the nine marks
A measured census showing star-like defects are rare, or common, on original negatives

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E005 documents the contact-printing chain, from critics who built one of the digitizations. Both datasets were scanned from copy negatives printed from the same intermediate positive, and the pathway is not disputed. TRN-E023 qualifies its reach. For the two flagship events the marks are reported on the original, so the mechanism no longer explains them, though it stands for the uninspected catalog. The pathway is established; its rate is not.

treatment.plainLanguage: The two modern scans of the survey both descend from the same intermediate copy, so a flaw made at that copying step would show up in both.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It dissolves 'found in two independent datasets' for the whole catalog. It no longer reaches the canonical events if the original-plate report holds (TRN-E022, on TRN-C024). Without a rate it cannot say how many candidates it explains.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E023: the flagship marks are not confined to copy material, so for the events fought hardest the mechanism does not apply.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A per-generation census showing star-like marks are rarely introduced at the copy stage
Outside re-registration showing the flagship marks are absent from the original negative

claimAssessments.reasoning: Four concordant records support it. They are the discovery report (TRN-E001), the critics' physical inspection of the Edinburgh copy (TRN-E002, strong), an independent pipeline recovering eight of nine (TRN-E008), and the microscopy study on the original (TRN-E022). The critics' confirmation is the decisive one, because it comes from the side with reason to doubt.

treatment.plainLanguage: Nine star-like dots really are on the surviving copies of the 12 April 1950 plate, and on nothing photographed before or since.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Every account accepts it; it establishes that there is something to explain, not what explains it.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E002 also found similar appear-once detections on the neighbouring plate and ordinary blemishes on both, so presence alone does not set these marks apart.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A deep modern image recovering a persistent source at one of the positions
Evidence that the Edinburgh inspection or the pipeline recovery mis-registered the positions

claimAssessments.reasoning: One record, TRN-E022, supports it. Microscopy of the Caltech original, registered against the digitization, finds all nine at their positions. The text was read in full and checked verbatim, but it is an unreviewed preprint. The examination was unblinded, the group includes the hypothesis's chief proponent, and nobody outside has repeated the registration. The microscopist was directed to the objects by the copy-defect argument's author, which gives the location some cross-camp standing.

treatment.plainLanguage: All nine 1950 dots are on the original glass negative that was in the telescope, not only on later copies.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It removes the copying-chain explanation for the flagship event, but it does not separate a flash from a flaw born in the original emulsion (TRN-E024, on TRN-C020).
treatment.strongestObjection: The registration is unblinded, unreviewed and by an interested group; the step that carries the conclusion has not been independently checked.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blinded outside re-registration of the Caltech plate
Publication with the registration images available for inspection

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E003 (strong) gives the profile statistics. All nine fall on the sharp side of the stellar distribution, with joint odds of order 0.1^9 if they were stars, and they look more concentrated under the microscope. The measurement is common ground; TRN-E004 and TRN-E006 dispute only what it means.

treatment.plainLanguage: The nine 1950 dots are tighter and more concentrated than real stars of the same brightness on the same plate.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It can be read as a defect signature (TRN-E004) or a flash signature (TRN-E006). With no calibration of how either looks on period emulsion, it points neither way.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E004's classifier defines its spurious class by lack of a modern counterpart, the property that defines every transient candidate, so its artifact reading is circular.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A flash-profile calibration showing whether sub-second flashes produce these profiles
A defect census showing whether emulsion flaws occupy the same profile range

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E007 (peer reviewed) reports the triple on one exposure, absent from the next within the hour and from 2023 imaging to magnitude 25.5. TRN-E008 recovers all three independently. TRN-E022 finds the triple on a Harvard copy plate and in the original digitization. Confidence is moderate because the 1952 original negative itself has not been examined.

treatment.plainLanguage: Three bright dots appeared close together on a July 1952 plate, were gone from the next exposure less than an hour later, and have never reappeared.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It establishes a second event to explain. Its star-like profiles differ from the sharper 1950 nine, a tension any single mechanism must absorb.
treatment.strongestObjection: No physical inspection of the 1952 original negative; presence there is inferred from the digitization (TRN-E022's own limitation).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Microscopy of the 1952 original negative
A persistent faint counterpart found at the position

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E008 (strong) describes a from-scratch pipeline. It recovers 8 of 9 and 3 of 3 canonical sources and 63.9% of the 5,399 catalog, with low false positives in control fields. TRN-E016 is context on how that catalog was built. The software is independent; the digitized material is the same.

treatment.plainLanguage: Software written by an outsider, without the discoverers' code or lists, finds the same flagship dots and most of the published catalog.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It rules out software error as the source of the marks, but says nothing about light versus flaw, since both would be on the scans.
treatment.strongestObjection: It uses the same digitized copies as the original team; independence of software is not independence of material.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A second independent pipeline failing to recover the canonical sources

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone, with no admitted evidence record. The anchor is Watters et al.'s summary that decades of gamma-ray-burst plate searches produced no confident identification. That is a statement about outcomes, not a measured defect rate. The critics' observation of blemishes on copy plates, filed under the 1950 event, shows defects exist, not their rate or how star-like they are. The claim is plausible on priors; the rate is unmeasured.

treatment.plainLanguage: Ordinary flaws from the emulsion, copying and scanning make star-like dots often enough to swamp a search for one-time flashes.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If measured high, it would absorb most of the catalog. If measured low, it would force the defect account to explain clustered, star-like marks it currently cannot.
treatment.strongestObjection: No census exists (TRN-R007 is unrun), and the account has no reach over the Hamburg archive, which shares no copying chain with Palomar.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A per-generation defect census on archives where several copy generations survive
Injection-recovery on blank plate regions measuring the rate of star-like false detections

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: the proponents' profiles preprint states it as a consequence of optics and seeing. The same argument appears in the proponents' reply filed against the sharpness claim, and that reply is itself an argument, not a measurement. No one has exposed period emulsion to controlled flashes. It is physically plausible as a prior, and untested.

treatment.plainLanguage: A flash lasting under a second should leave a sharper, rounder dot than a star, because stars are smeared by the air and by tracking over a long exposure.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A calibration would turn the sharpness measurement into evidence in whichever direction it falls; for now the argument only neutralises the defect reading of TRN-C002.
treatment.strongestObjection: Flash and defect profile distributions may overlap entirely, in which case sharpness discriminates nothing.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A Schmidt-emulsion calibration with controlled millisecond-to-second flashes beside artificial stars

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E013 reports appear-once candidates with narrow profiles on 41 Hamburg Schmidt plates from 1954–57, labelled preliminary by the author. It is credible as a report of candidates on an independent archive. It has no false-positive calibration, no injection testing and no rate against matched controls.

treatment.plainLanguage: Similar one-time dots show up on plates from Hamburg Observatory, a different telescope, emulsion and archive with no shared copies.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It escapes the Palomar copying chain entirely, but without a measured rate it cannot separate the same phenomenon from the same defect susceptibility.
treatment.strongestObjection: Old emulsions may fail in similar ways everywhere; examples without matched-control rates show recurrence, not a sky origin.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A candidate rate above matched-control defect rates, with injection-recovery completeness
The same excess rate found in a third archive

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E014 reports coma patterns on Hamburg candidates from a telescope chosen for strong off-axis coma. Its author states the data do not establish the light's origin. It is a single-author preprint with an unvalidated classifier, and defect classes that mimic asymmetry have not been excluded. The grade is provisional because a careful method reports the observation, not because anyone has checked it.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some Hamburg dots carry the small comet-shaped smear the telescope's optics give real off-axis light, which scratches and chemical flaws should not have.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It is the only physical light-versus-flaw test in the record. If validated it would decide TRN-C020 for those candidates and be usable across archives; it does not touch the Palomar events.
treatment.strongestObjection: It is not blind-validated, and directional defects such as drying marks or development streaks could mimic coma asymmetry.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A frozen blind test separating deliberately produced flashes from the full catalog of defects
The classifier failing that test

claimAssessments.reasoning: In support: independent code on the author-supplied rows reproduces 0.46% against about 1.4% (TRN-E010). The deficit persists among ML-scored likelier-real candidates (TRN-E015), and TRN-E017 closes one environmental route. Against: TRN-E011 (strong) shows the assumed uniform background is false and finds no significant deficit under a proper null in closely related datasets. TRN-E051 concedes spatial non-uniformity; TRN-E012 argues Watters' subset is underpowered. Everything in favour uses one catalog. The grade is mixed rather than weak because the critique's datasets are proxies.

treatment.plainLanguage: The catalog has fewer candidates inside Earth's shadow, at satellite height, than chance would give — what sunlit reflectors would produce.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It would weigh heavily against the defect account if it survived on an independent catalog; it gives nothing between natural and artificial reflectors.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E011: with a background that rises toward plate corners and edges, the deficit is not significant.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered shadow analysis across independently extracted catalogs finding the deficit
The deficit vanishing on Hayes's independent catalog

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E052 and TRN-E053 report the deficit larger at every assumed altitude after filtering to p>0.7, reaching 0.805 at 35,000 km. The source supports the claim as stated. Its meaning is limited: the filter and the catalog are the same group's, and few filtered candidates fall in shadow at high altitudes.

treatment.plainLanguage: When likely defects are filtered out, the shortfall of candidates inside Earth's shadow gets stronger, not weaker.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It would favour a real signal if the filter were independent. But a classifier that removes defect-like rows sharpens any signal defects dilute, real or not.
treatment.strongestObjection: Only 17 filtered candidates fall in shadow at 35,000 km and above, and the filter is trained on the group's own visual labels.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The same strengthening with a filter trained on physical ground truth
The same result on an independently extracted catalog

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone, with no admitted evidence record. Its disclosed basis lies on sibling claims. The shell fit prefers 20,000 km on the full catalog but fits poorly (TRN-E055, on TRN-C107), and the recomputed deficit peaks at 25,000 km (TRN-E025, on TRN-C105). The authors state the range is a spread across choices, not a confidence interval, and the model omits orbital motion. It also presupposes TRN-C005 and TRN-C021.

treatment.plainLanguage: The reflecting objects, if real, lie mostly between 20,000 and 35,000 km above Earth.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It refines the near-Earth account without testing it. It matters mainly because the hotspot locations of TRN-C119 depend on the assumed altitude.
treatment.strongestObjection: The best fit has a reduced χ² of 3.5–5.4 and no formal interval, and the preferred altitude moves with sample and cut.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered fit with orbital dynamics and independent shadow code giving overlapping intervals on three catalogs, including an independent one

claimAssessments.reasoning: It reproduces on the original rows with independent code, controls and a permutation test (TRN-E010). It persists among likelier-real candidates (TRN-E015) and survives an autocorrelated Bayesian model, attenuated (TRN-E019); TRN-E017 closes one confounder. But the only independently extracted catalog finds a relative risk of 1.35 with an interval spanning 1, and an exposure-weighted IRR of 1.03 (TRN-E009). TRN-E011 ties the timing to the observing schedule. TRN-E012 disputes the critique's power.

treatment.plainLanguage: More candidates show up on plates taken within a day of atmospheric nuclear weapons tests.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Even if real, fallout reaching the plates and glinting objects predict it equally, so it cannot select among accounts.
treatment.strongestObjection: TRN-E009: rebuilt from scratch with nightly sky coverage modelled, the effect is null.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered exposure-denominator analysis built from raw plate logs
A plate-level audit of the Castle Yankee night showing candidates spread across many plates with star-like images

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone: Cann's preprint reports a dose-response from 17.4% to 2.4% across Kp bins, and no admitted evidence record carries it. TRN-E017, attached to TRN-C006 and TRN-C005, shows plate sensitivity does not vary with storms. That closes one artifact route but does not establish this association. The claim comes from the same catalog lineage.

treatment.plainLanguage: Fewer candidates appear during geomagnetic storms, and allowing for that makes the nuclear-test link stronger.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It is an association inside the contested catalog. An environmental effect on plates or processing could produce it as readily as a physical population.
treatment.strongestObjection: The paper's tables have not been extracted and checked, and the catalog is the contested working set.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The same dose-response on an independently extracted catalog
The paper's tables admitted as checked evidence

claimAssessments.reasoning: Held on its anchor alone. The source paper has not been read in full, and the characterisation comes from its title and a critic's discussion. A second, related alignment preprint (weak, qualifying) is filed against other claims and is not counted here. No admitted record carries this proposition.

treatment.plainLanguage: Some groups of one-time dots are reported to lie in straight lines, as a moving object flashing repeatedly might leave.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Alignments inherit the marks' provenance: if the marks are defects, so are the lines.
treatment.strongestObjection: Look-elsewhere inflation: alignment criteria chosen after the fact over many plates.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A preregistered alignment search with a stated trials factor on an independent catalog
The source paper read in full and its alignment statistics checked

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E041 reports 16 of 137 cells significant after Bonferroni correction against the group's own plate-aware control. TRN-E078 describes the fixed-altitude projection method. As a statement of what the analysis returned, the claim is supported; its meaning is weak. The locations depend on the assumed 35,786 km altitude, and the catalog and filter are those of every group result.

treatment.plainLanguage: Projected onto a shell at satellite height, candidates bunch over 16 patches of Earth more than random positions would, even after correcting for testing many patches.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: A plate with a high defect rate projects its excess wherever the geometry sends it, so hotspot significance is not a test of the sky.
treatment.strongestObjection: At the 20,000 km the companion estimator prefers, the same candidates fall into different cells (TRN-E078's projection dependence).
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The same regions recurring across altitudes, grids and Hayes's independent catalog

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E079 reports the first random control reaching silhouette 0.50, 'just meeting' the authors' criterion for non-random clustering; the other controls reach 0.50–0.60. The authors' own figures support the claim as stated. Only three draws were run, so there is no null distribution.

treatment.plainLanguage: Random positions put through the same clustering method also pass the test the authors use to call clustering non-random.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It undercuts the clustering method as a test of sky structure. It bears on the hotspot results, not on whether the marks are light.
treatment.strongestObjection: Three draws are too few to know where the real value of 0.70 sits in the control distribution.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A thousand-draw null distribution in which 0.70 lies far in the tail

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E038 states the mismatch between millimetre plasma grains and inferred facet sizes. That size inference (TRN-C111) is built from assumed altitude, specularity, duration and reflectivity. Its authors concede that bright-source exclusion biases it toward small sizes (TRN-E062, TRN-E063, on TRN-C111). Cann's mechanism is not modelled directly. On the parent TRN-C021, Cann's own flux argument gives icy aggregates 1–4 m across (TRN-E020).

treatment.plainLanguage: The tiny dust grains of the natural 'dusty plasma' idea seem far too small to make flashes this bright, so that idea is ruled out unless the size estimate changes.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: It would favour the artificial over the natural near-Earth account, but only through a selection-biased toy model.
treatment.strongestObjection: Cann proposes aggregates metres across, not single millimetre grains, so the comparison may be between different objects.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A size inference from a catalog that includes bright sources
A direct model of aggregate reflectivity compared with the observed magnitudes

claimAssessments.reasoning: TRN-E072 reports the toy-model conclusion, and TRN-E073 records the authors' caveat. It argues from residual fit among models the authors chose. Its premises are features graded mixed here (TRN-C005, TRN-C006) or held on anchors (TRN-C103, TRN-C104), plus one read both ways (TRN-C002). It is weakly supported as a statement of what the models do; it is not a test.

treatment.plainLanguage: Among the few explanations the proponents modelled, only one involving non-human intelligence fits all five features they report.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Residual fit among a hand-picked set: adding one natural model, or removing one contested feature, changes the answer.
treatment.strongestObjection: Three of the five features are contested at the catalog level; fitting contested features is not evidence.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: The five features established on an independent catalog and a range of natural models shown to fail them
